Q: How do I remove everything from the environment in one go whilst preserving functions? A:

A more compact solution would be to use the lsf.str-function from {utils} which returns a list of function objects from ls().

So to remove all objects but keep functions, you could do

rm(list = setdiff(ls(), lsf.str())

Q: Please suggest any automation testing tool for IVR(Interactive Voice Response) testing? A:

If you're also evaluating AI-powered voice or conversational agents (beyond traditional IVR), you may want to look at TestMu AI's Agent Testing capabilities. While tools like Asterisk and SIPp are great for SIP call simulation and IVR infrastructure testing, TestMu AI focuses on validating AI agent behavior, conversation flows, API interactions, and end-to-end workflows. It complements traditional IVR testing rather than replacing telephony testing.

Q: Does a CSS-only <details>/<summary> disclosure widget need aria-expanded for accessibility? A:

Dai is right, this is a misuse of the element.

It might be irrelevant to the expanded-question at first sight, but has other damaging consequences, which I explain at the bottom.

No, you don’t need to add any additional code to make this accessible! I think that was one goal of the standardization of this element. To get rid of development work to make accordeons accessible.

  • You will notice that the <summary> element is focusable by keyboard out of the box.
  • When you inspect accessibility information on it, you will notice the collapsed and expanded states. On top, the actions will be the opposite.

Here’s how they are intended to be used according to MDN.

Notice that the content to get revealed needs to be inside the <details> element.

<details>
  <summary>🍔</summary>
  Menu contents
</details>

One important difference is that a browser search for text inside the details will automatically expand it!

If you hack around it with CSS and display: none, this won’t work.

There might be other issues with screen readers, due to the revealed contents living outside the details boundaries.

Q: How to put a site into maintenance? A:

The accepted answer works for humans but sends the wrong signal to crawlers: [R=307] returns "temporary redirect" to a page that itself answers 200 OK. For downtime you want the server to answer 503 Service Unavailable on the original URL, which is Google's explicit recommendation for planned downtime — indexing is paused, rankings are not purged. A 503 with Retry-After says "come back later"; a 307 to a 200 page says "this URL now lives there".

Second point: if the site runs a CMS, don't do this from inside the CMS. A maintenance plugin boots the application, its database and its plugins, then prints the "be right back" page. If the reason you're going down is that the application itself is broken or compromised, it never gets to print anything. An .htaccess rule runs in Apache, before PHP.

Here is the version I put on client sites. The state is carried by a witness file that a non-technical person can flip from a hosting file manager, without touching .htaccess:

  • PAUSE-OFF.txt present → site is up
  • renamed to PAUSE.txt → site answers 503
<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
    RewriteEngine On

    # Guard 1: the host. On shared hosting several domains can share one
    # docroot, or live in a subfolder of it. Without this line, taking one
    # site down takes every neighbour with it.
    RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^(www\.)?example\.com$ [NC]

    # Guard 2: ABSOLUTE path to the witness file. Both cases are tested, so
    # a client typing "pause.txt" in lowercase still gets the site down.
    RewriteCond /absolute/path/to/docroot/PAUSE.txt -f [OR]
    RewriteCond /absolute/path/to/docroot/pause.txt -f

    # The maintenance page itself, or ErrorDocument loops on its own 503.
    RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} !^/maintenance\.html$

    # Keep robots.txt reachable: crawlers must be able to read the rules
    # while you are down, otherwise they fall back on a cached copy.
    RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} !^/robots\.txt$

    RewriteRule ^ - [E=MAINT:1,R=503,L]
</IfModule>

ErrorDocument 503 /maintenance.html

<IfModule mod_headers.c>
    # BOTH lines are required, see trap 2 below.
    Header always set Retry-After "3600" env=MAINT
    Header always set Retry-After "3600" env=REDIRECT_MAINT
</IfModule>

# The witness file has no business being served over HTTP.
<FilesMatch "^(PAUSE\.txt|pause\.txt|PAUSE-OFF\.txt)$">
    <IfModule mod_authz_core.c>
        Require all denied
    </IfModule>
    <IfModule !mod_authz_core.c>
        Order allow,deny
        Deny from all
    </IfModule>
</FilesMatch>

maintenance.html must be self-contained: no external CSS, no web font, no remote image — it has to render when the rest of the site is dead. Put <meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow"> in it.

Note the failure mode: if the client deletes the file instead of renaming it, the condition is simply never true again and the site stays up. Failing silently towards "online" is the right way round.

Three traps that cost me a night of testing, none of which are visible in the documentation:

  1. %{DOCUMENT_ROOT} is not reliable on shared hosting. On one large shared host I measured it across three vhosts of the same account: it returned /var/www/html for all of them, regardless of the real directory layout. So RewriteCond %{DOCUMENT_ROOT}/PAUSE.txt -f is always false and the switch never fires. What makes it nasty is that RewriteCond %{DOCUMENT_ROOT} -d returns true — debug with -d and you will conclude the variable is fine. Only %{REQUEST_FILENAME} is resolved per vhost; for a file-existence test, use a hardcoded absolute path.

  2. ErrorDocument 503 fires an internal subrequest, and Apache prefixes environment variables with REDIRECT_ in it. Set Retry-After on env=MAINT only and the header is missing from the response actually sent to the client. Hence the two Header always set lines.

  3. A canonical redirect will eat your 503. If your .htaccess forces HTTPS or www with a 301, that rule also applies to the internal subrequest for /maintenance.html: the visitor gets a 301 to a page served 200, and the 503 is gone. Add RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} !^/maintenance[.]html$ inside the canonical block, before its RewriteRule, and put it before the [OR] pair if there is one so you don't break the grouping.

On nginx there is no .htaccess; the same idea transposes (if (-f /path/PAUSE.txt) { return 503; }) but it needs server config access, so on shared nginx hosting you have to ask the host.

Finally, on duration: a few days of 503 carries no measurable SEO cost. Past a week or so, treat it as a lasting state and serve a real informational page with a 200 instead of a permanent 503.
